Esteve CDMO, the CDMO arm of Spanish pharmaceutical CDMO, is planning to spend over $80 million to relocate, expand and modernise its operations in China. It will open a new site in Shaoxing, featuring three manufacturing workshops with a total volume of 250 m³, plus the space to add 150 m³ as demand growns.
“Strengthening our presence in China allows us to bring our capabilities closer to customers in Asia while leveraging the expertise of our global network,” said Joan Petit, president of Esteve CDMO. The company has been in China, where it offers technologies including spray drying and HPAPI manufacturing for the Chinese and wider Asian markets.
Earlier, the company approved a $17.5 million investment at its site in Morton Grove, Illinois, bringing the total his year to $33 million. This will include two new 1,900L reactors, enhanced laboratory containment capabilities and a warehouse revamp. The stated aim is to increase flexibility in early development and expanding manufacturing capacity as programmes progress toward larger clinical and commercial requirements.

articles.title_orig: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.
articles.title_zh: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.
articles.content_orig:
PepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said on Thursday.
The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain KFC said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements.
Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category.
Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC.
Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants.
The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

articles.title_orig: France's Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest
articles.title_zh: France's Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest
articles.content_orig:
Officers are instruments of state whose job is to repress, rather than manage, public dissent
Familiar images of teargas clouds drifting across Paris squares, police baton charges against masked protesters and terrified teenagers floored – and worse – by stun grenades have once again focused the world’s attention on France’s policing methods.
While most of its western European neighbours generally favour police tactics that prioritise crowd containment and de-escalation, France has long responded to social movements that take to the streets with, at times, shocking physical force.
The reasons why are a complex mix of history, politics, state organisation and a particular security culture that has become deeply ingrained over decades, if not centuries, and whose limits continue to be pushed today.
French policing policy is rooted in Napoleon’s ultra-centralised state and in the political philosophy of the Republic. In France, the police are an instrument of the state. Their core task is to protect it, enforce its laws, and maintain public order.
Conceptually, that is a far cry from, for example, the UK, where since the early 1800s the police have been considered servants of the public, whose authority derives from public consent and whose chief responsibility is to keep the peace.
French police officers are agents of state authority. That means protests, blockades and mass disorder are not just civil nuisances, but direct challenges to the authority of the republic. The police’s priority is to reclaim the streets, not to negotiate.
That explains the aggressive tactics, such as systematically encircling and trapping crowds, and the continued use of “intermediate” or less-than-lethal weapons, many of which are banned or heavily restricted elsewhere in Europe.
Defence ball launchers, for example, fire rubber projectiles at 185mph (300kph). The explosive grenades that injured gilets jaunes protesters in the late 2010s and killed an environmental protester in 2014 have been phased out, but been replaced by pyrotechnic stun grenades.
Designed to disperse crowds through both impact and a 160dB acoustic shock, these have caused multiple injuries in recent years, including lost eyes and teeth, fractured jaws and several amputated limbs . They also frequently instil mass panic.
Violent policing methods are also fostered by France’s almost unique culture of street protest. A legacy of insurrection dating back to the 1789 revolution means protesters know the street can, and generally does, force governments to back down.
Unlike in Germany or the Netherlands, French unions, while they may strike often, are not formal government negotiating partners. The top-heavy, presidential structure of the Fifth Republic also marginalises institutional consultation.
All that means a heavily centralised state may pass laws with little popular consent, making the “power of the street” one of citizens’ few viable means of winning concessions. Protest, here, is regarded as a civic duty and a legitimate democratic tool .
That creates a vicious circle. French authorities see large crowds as an existential threat, so send in the police. Their military-style tactics antagonise even peaceful demonstrators, and validates more radical groups in their violence.
And rather than trying to contain and isolate those violent elements, police respond with baton charges and munitions. The aggression is entrenched – and protests turn into pitched battles between citizens and police.
after newsletter promotion
Data from conflict monitoring organisations, such as Acled, consistently shows that France, perhaps surprisingly, does not always record western Europe’s highest number of demonstrations (Germany and Italy also vie for that title).
But it does show that France consistently records the highest rates of escalated, high-intensity unrest, including street barricades, widespread vandalism and looting, arson attacks and direct confrontations between protesters and police.
France’s approach to policing and crowd management has for decades drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors and civil society groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Council of Europe.
Reports have documented instances of excessive force, misuse of grenades and rubber bullets, arbitrary mass arrests and routine teargas deployment against largely non-violent protesters. But the model persists, and is even expanding.
Last month, thousands marched in protest at a proposed “licence to kill” law seeking to establish a legal “presumption of self-defence” for police officers and gendarmes using firearms in the line of duty.
The law, opposed by civil rights groups, leftwing politicians, the magistrates’ union and the UN, would in effect shift the burden of proof on to victims and their families to demonstrate that a police shooting was disproportionate.
In essence, critics argue, it would institutionalise police impunity; reinforcing, once more, a security culture that treats public dissent and social tension not as democratic realities to be managed, but as insurrections to be repressed. The battle for France’s streets is far from over.

Stocks tumbled slid on Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence companies, while while oil prices jumped as geopolitical tensions rise.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite pulled back 2.1%, while the S&P 500 shed 1.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 279 points, or 0.5%.
Meta Platforms slipped 6% even it exceeded revenue expectations and offered upbeat guidance. Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 5%, while Micron Technology and Nvidia dropped 2% and 1%, respectively.
Neocloud leader CoreWeave , whose bond yields and credit default swaps remain elevated , declined nearly 4% as well. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.
Huang's commentary about a scarcity of capital is "spooking markets and reigniting the concerns around the capital markets on the credit side being full from a risk appetite standpoint," said Wells Fargo traders in a note. They also said Meta's comments about the large amount of AI funding needed caused the shares to roll over and weighed on overall market.
JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."
Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.
Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. President Donald Trump also told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."
International benchmark Brent crude futures traded 3% higher at above $112.45 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude futures advanced 2% to above $99.95 per barrel.
Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped more than 9 basis points to 5.048%. The 2-year note yield also shed 9 basis points to trade at 4.733%.
Wolfe Research downgraded Netflix to peer perform from outperform.
Wolfe cited stagnant viewer engagement, intensifying streaming competition and concerns about the company's long-term growth prospects.
"Engagement failed to respond to rising investment, and last week's content leadership changes convince us that solutions require patience & lower incremental margins. Attention economy competition is rampant. Consensus estimates look fair. Downgrade to Peer Perform," Wolfe's analyst Peter Supino said.
The streaming giant has struggled, Supino said, to generate new hits despite increasing content spending by $3 billion over the past two years. The firm also removed its $95 price target.
Despite $3B of content expense growth over the last two years, "Netflix has lost its mojo" according to Supino. The analyst pointed to growing competition from YouTube and rival streaming platforms, adding  that higher programming costs may weigh on Netflix's future profit margins. Recent changes to Netflix's content leadership could help, but improvements will likely take time.
"In a not unreasonable downside scenario where Netflix revenue decelerates to MSD by 2030 (not our base case), we think NFLX would be worth ~$50/shr. today, and therefore do not think LT engagement / growth concerns are fully priced in," Supino said.

He also favors CME's launch of a series of new products, which could "evolve into larger opportunities," citing its successful launch of its crypto futures service.
The analyst also cites CME's expansion in some cases to 24/7 trading for pre-existing retail-sized contracts.
Rollins reported weaker-than-expected third-quarter results as the pest control company continued to face challenges attracting residential customers.
Revenue rose 6.2% from a year earlier to $1.09 billion, while adjusted earnings came in at 33 cents per share. Analysts polled by FactSet expected a profit of 34 cents per share on revenue of $1.11 billion.
"We are disappointed with our third quarter performance and are acting with urgency to address the challenges impacting our results. We now have a clearer understanding of how the customer acquisition landscape is evolving and are taking concrete steps to optimize our approach," said President and CEO Jerry Gahlhoff Jr.
To be sure, the stock rose more than 4%.

articles.title_orig: Amex Platinum adds Airbnb perks and credits, ends one-night hotel credits
articles.title_zh: Amex Platinum adds Airbnb perks and credits, ends one-night hotel credits
articles.content_orig:
Card benefits are always evolving, and today, it's American Express's turn to announce some changes to one of the big benefits on the American Express Platinum Card® and The Business Platinum Card® from American Express .
Most of the changes are good news, though one may disappoint cardmembers who enjoy using their statement credits for one-night hotel stays.
Let's start with the good news: Amex is adding more than 1 million Airbnb listings to its American Express Travel® booking platform and expanding the Platinum card's newly renamed up to $600 annual lodging statement credit to include select Airbnb Luxe stays. There's also a new up to $250 Airbnb Experiences statement credit you can potentially unlock with those stays.
Here's what you need to know.
Find out your Amex Platinum Card offer: New cardmembers can find out their offer and see if they are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)
Eligible cardmembers can now earn American Express Membership Rewards points on prepaid Airbnb stays booked through Amex Travel or the Amex Travel App™.
Platinum or Business Platinum cardmembers will earn 5 points per dollar spent on eligible bookings, including both Airbnb Luxe and non-Luxe properties.
Based on TPG's October 2026 valuations that value Membership Rewards points at 2 cents each, that's a 10% return on spending in the form of Membership Rewards points, which is pretty solid.
Most other eligible Membership Rewards cards will earn 2 points per dollar spent on prepaid Airbnb bookings through Amex Travel or the Amex Travel App.
And while earning bonus points is always nice, being able to use statement credits is even better. That's where two additional changes to the Platinum's benefits come into play.
The Amex Platinum's up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (formerly the $600 hotel statement credit) is split into two up to $300 biannual statement credits — one from January through June and the other from July through December.
The statement credit can now be used toward eligible prepaid Airbnb Luxe stays booked through Amex Travel or the Amex Travel App, in addition to qualifying Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings.
To use one of these up to $300 statement credits on an Airbnb stay, you'll need to book through Amex Travel and stay at least two nights and select a property that's part of Airbnb Luxe.
Airbnb describes its Luxe properties as "private homes in sought-after destinations around the world, each selected by Airbnb for its quality, design and distinctive setting."
In my test searches, Luxe properties made up only a small subset of Airbnb listings. But there are certainly some options where a $300 statement credit could go a long way toward a two-night stay, including this example I found in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, where two nights later this year cost $874.
Assuming the booking meets the statement credit's eligibility requirements, the stay could drop to just $574 for two nights at a pretty great-looking spot with three bedrooms in the Smokies.
If you book an eligible prepaid Airbnb Luxe stay through Amex Travel using your Platinum or Business Platinum Card, you'll unlock access to an all-new up to $250 annual statement credit for eligible Airbnb Experiences, whether or not you use your lodging credit toward the stay.
This additional credit can be unlocked once per calendar year and is valid for the remainder of that year. Unlike the lodging credit, Airbnb Experiences can be booked directly through Airbnb.
In my searches, Airbnb Experiences cover a wide range of activities, including paddleboarding, airboat rides, sunset cruises, walking tours, food tours and cultural experiences.
Prices for some experiences start around $10 to $20, while private tours and other higher-end activities can cost several hundred dollars. In other words, $250 could go a long way towards an experience.
There's also some flexibility here: Your Airbnb Experience doesn't need to take place during your Luxe stay or even in the same destination. It can happen before or after your stay, and even in a future calendar year, as long as you purchase it after your Luxe booking is confirmed and before the end of the calendar year.
There's no minimum spending requirement for an eligible Airbnb Experience, so you can use the credit toward smaller purchases or an eligible Experience costing $250 or more.
For 2026, that means cardmembers who book a qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe stay now can unlock up to $250 in statement credits for eligible Airbnb Experiences purchased by Dec. 31 — even if the experience itself takes place in 2027.
More ways to use existing credits and new credits to unlock are certainly good news.
But as Amex expands the ways to use the Platinum's newly renamed $600 annual lodging statement credit, it's also making a change that won't be welcome news for everyone.
Previously, stays booked through The Hotel Collection ( which I recently tried and loved ) required at least two nights to use the Platinum's lodging credit. However, Fine Hotels + Resorts stays had no minimum stay requirement, meaning you could use an up to $300 credit toward a stay of just one night.
Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, all eligible uses of the Platinum's lodging statement credit will require stays of at least two nights, whether you're booking through Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe. You can still get Fine Hotels + Resorts benefits on one-night stays, just not utilize the lodging credit.
This creates a consistent requirement across all three booking options, but it's still probably disappointing news for cardholders who have enjoyed using their credits toward one-night Fine Hotels + Resorts stays.
The good news is that if you still have one of this year's up to $300 statement credits burning a hole in your pocket, you can still use it toward an eligible one-night Fine Hotels + Resorts stay before the new requirement takes effect in 2027.
Related: How I used my Fine Hotels + Resorts credit and came out $1 ahead
If you use the major credits and benefits, it's possible to get substantially more value from the American Express Platinum and Business Platinum Cards each year than you pay in annual fees.
But the key to doing that is taking advantage of major credits and benefits like the newly renamed $600 annual lodging statement credit — and potentially even unlocking another $250 in Airbnb Experiences statement credits.
Having more ways to use those credits is certainly welcome news. However, cardholders who have gotten used to using their credits for one-night Fine Hotels + Resorts stays will, unfortunately, need a new strategy beginning next year.
Let us know in the comments how these changes impact your strategy and what you think of the new Airbnb Luxe and Experiences options.

BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways.
The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
“You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.
“So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.
Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.
But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast .
The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.
About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island , which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.
“We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.
The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.
A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.
More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.
These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran  prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz —  cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.
That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.
The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.
But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.
The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.
Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.
“They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.
“They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.”
But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.”
Using tribal power and rigorous detective work, a family of an army officer in Yemen tries to find out how he was abducted in broad daylight, and what happened to him afterward.
In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen’s coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control.
In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen’s road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars.
Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen’s coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area.

articles.title_orig: Cruise lines chase luxury travelers with suites for up to $25,000 a night
articles.title_zh: Cruise lines chase luxury travelers with suites for up to $25,000 a night
articles.content_orig:
The latest push into high-end travel is taking place on the high seas, as cruise lines increasingly lean on luxury offerings.
On Regent's Seven Seas Splendor, an all-luxury ship, cabins cost anywhere from $1,800 to $15,000 per night for its top-of-the-line booking, the Regent Suite.
The difference is not just the roughly 5,100 square feet of space. The top-tier suite has a Steinway piano, a private dining room reserved for its occupants, and a wraparound deck with a hot tub and a view comparable to the one from the ship's bridge.
Multiple passengers wanted the suite for Splendor’s 151-night global cruise that embarks in January, Regent told CNBC, and it is almost always occupied.
Regent is setting its sights even bigger, as the cruise line plans to debut Seven Seas Prestige in December, its first new ship class in a decade. Its top suite costs $25,000 per night.
While mega-ships with surfing and water slides can carry more than 7,500 passengers, the smaller, elite ships — some carrying fewer than a thousand passengers — are powering profits for companies like Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings . The company owns luxury lines Regent and Oceania.
Norwegian CEO John Chidsey has said he's focused on sharpening the luxury brands' positioning, improving the products and guest experience, and strengthening their commercial performance.
Regent and Oceania, he said, are in good shape for 2027, though Chidsey did not break out metrics between the companies.
Cruise competitors are also betting big on luxury offerings, investing in new ships and more specialized experiences.
Regent competes with established luxury cruise lines including Royal Caribbean's Silversea and Carnival's Seabourn, as well as newer entrants carrying hotel names into the market. Four Seasons, Aman and Orient Express are among the brands bringing luxury hospitality to yacht-style vessels.
The cruise industry projects the luxury cruise fleet will grow from 104 ships in 2026 to at least 130 by 2036.
And while global cruise passengers are forecast to increase about 11% between 2025 and 2028, according to the Cruise Lines International Association, or CLIA, the industry's investment dollars are increasingly flowing to luxury and expedition brands, with orders rising for smaller ships and fewer berths through the next decade.
From 2020 through 2025, there has been a 71% increase in the number of luxury ships and an 84% increase in berths, according to CLIA. The orders indicate another 26% jump in number of ships through the end of 2029 and a 32% increase in capacity.
Other hospitality companies are investing and expanding their uber-upscale offerings, too. Hotels, casinos, airlines, restaurants, spas and other travel and leisure companies see the trend: Affluent customers remain willing to pay for more space , personal service and distinctive experiences.
United Airlines this year launched its larger Polaris Studio suites with privacy doors and caviar service. American Airlines increased its lie-flat capacity and reported on Thursday that its premium passenger unit revenue rose 18.5% in the third quarter, compared with 14.4% in its main cabin.
Marriott’s second-quarter results showed luxury revenue per available room growing faster than the broader hotel business in the U.S. and Canada, rising 9.1% year over year, compared with 5% for all Marriott hotels in the region. In June, CEO Anthony Capuano told CNBC there's an “almost insatiable appetite” for luxury travel.
Wynn Resorts, which caters almost exclusively to high-end customers, has opted to maintain its high room rates in Las Vegas even as visitation has slowed over the past year, rather than filling every room with travelers looking for a bargain.
Asked onstage at the Global Gaming Expo in September whether Wynn is extracting more profit from fewer customers, CEO Craig Billings said, "We will always focus on what's the most comfortable experience for the customer and where can we drive the highest possible EBITDA."
But offering luxury vacations doesn't guarantee a company's fortunes.
The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, for instance, has struggled with occupancy despite major marketing campaigns and has accumulated nearly $700 million in losses since 2017, according to the Financial Times.
More competition in the space could undercut the perception of scarcity. As more companies add luxury products, they have to convince travelers that the experience is worth the price.
Las Vegas Sands reported earnings Wednesday that missed expectations for revenue and profit, hurt by the high-end segments in both Macao and Singapore.
"When the customers don't show up, it's a little problematic," CEO Patrick Dumont said on the company's  earnings call.
Dumont said he couldn't point to any single cause for the softness, adding, "perhaps people are not feeling as good about the market," but he said he believes this quarter is an aberration.
CNBC asked Dumont during the NBA China Games in Macao on Oct. 9 whether luxury travel could become overcrowded.
In response, he pointed to the long-term wealth creation in Asia and said the challenge was making experiences customers want to return to.
“It’s not about, are there enough customers,” he said. “It’s, can we create enough of an interesting set of experiences where people find us indispensable in their lives.”

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials , though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News .
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters .
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X .
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used.  Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.

Warhammer Tone Pro: Superb coverage and vibrant colours
The Warhammer Tone Pro range lands on the shelf on Saturday. Yesterday, we saw just how flexible the new paints are , and today we’re looking at their coverage and vibrancy.
One of the first things you’ll notice when you open a pot of Tone Pro is how smooth and consistent the paint is, and all 150 paints have the same consistency. Then, when you’ve got the paint onto your brush, you’ll feel how smoothly it flows onto your miniatures.
The paints give incredible coverage – it’s the best coverage so far from a Warhammer paint. Even white* and yellow, which are notoriously difficult colours to get right, give a solid, opaque coat from the first application. The quality of the pigment in the paint is what allows it to cover so well, and it makes painting even those notorious colours much more accessible.

This really opens up your options for creativity and the different stories you can tell with your miniatures. Finally, the new paints will self-level as they dry. This means you’ll get a really smooth finish, brush strokes will disappear, and the details on your miniatures don’t get clogged up. This makes Tone Pro both easy to use and incredibly forgiving.
You’ll be able to get your hands on the new paints from Saturday. Head down to your local store to begin a new era of Warhammer painting.

Recalled oysters were distributed to restaurants and retailers across the country, and the company said they have alerted customers of the outbreak.
In addition to the recall, the Virginia Department of Health has also closed the Little Wicomico River harvest area as a precaution, the CDC said.
“Little Wicomico Oyster Company has stopped harvesting from the affected area and is cooperating with public health officials. Oysters harvested from other Virginia growing areas are not part of this recall,” the agency said.

articles.title_orig: Sony reportedly exits UHD Blu-ray player market
articles.title_zh: Sony reportedly exits UHD Blu-ray player market
articles.content_orig:
Sony, it seems, is exiting the dedicated 4K UHD Blu-ray player market wholesale. According to a new report from Japanese blog Kunkoku ( via FlatpanelsHD ), sales of Sony's last standalone player, the UBP-X700/K, are ending as of October 22.
Taking a look over at Sony's official online store in both the US and Canada, the UBP-X700/K is listed as out of stock. According to Kunkoku, Sony's Japanese storefront specifically lists the item as one that "will not be restocked."
The UBP-X700/K was first released in May 2025, and, up to this point, it has served as the last purpose-built 4K UHD player from Sony. With the UBP-X800M2 having also been discontinued over a year ago, this leaves the PlayStation 5 line as Sony's only 4K UHD-compatible hardware out on the market.
The UBP-X700/K is a premium 4K UHD Blu-ray player from Sony that features Dolby Vision, HDR10, Dolby Atmos, DTS:X, Super Audio CD (SACD) playback, and more.
Sony, for its part, has been in the process of phasing out physical media products for some time now. The company previously withdrew from the dedicated CD and SACD player markets, and, earlier this year, it bowed out of the Blu-ray recorder market as well. Notably, Sony also announced the end of physical disc production for the PlayStation 5 video game console starting in January 2028.
On the whole, the 4K UHD Blu-ray player market is in a rough position. Both Samsung and LG have stopped producing new 4K UHD players, which left Sony as one of the last major players still in the space. With Sony reportedly out of the picture, this leaves Panasonic as the last tech titan still producing disc-based players.
...it's disheartening to see Sony -- the company that spearheaded the Blu-ray era itself -- abandon ship so unceremoniously.
On the bright side, a number of smaller companies have jumped onto the 4K UHD scene in recent months, with new hardware arriving from Krovatar , Laser , and Magnetar , among others. These players fill specific niches in the market, though they're unlikely to move significant numbers of units, at least in the short-to-medium-term future.
Overall, it's disheartening to see Sony -- the company that spearheaded the Blu-ray era itself -- abandon ship so unceremoniously. The company's decision to end production of PlayStation 5 discs has been met with significant backlash, and so it's possible, though less likely, that its decision to leave the dedicated 4K UHD player market will be met with some level of pushback, too.

articles.title_orig: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.title_zh: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.content_orig:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds
Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.
The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.
Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.
Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.
In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.
Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.
Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.
after newsletter promotion
While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.
“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

articles.title_zh: German youth plan France-style mass protests
articles.content_orig:
"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions , groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France , Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

articles.title_zh: ‘Gears Of War: E-Day’ Cost Xbox $500 Million, Says New Report
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive Games Gears Of War: E-Day PS5 The Coalition Xbox
Gears of War: E-Day is a terrific game and it has the highest Metacritic score of any entry in the franchise since the original Xbox 360 trilogy. But early estimates suggest the positive buzz has not resulted in blockbuster sales numbers. That makes it an interesting test case for Xbox’s return to exclusivity, especially for a game that cost so much.
The first rumors of Gears of War: E-Day ‘s budget arose in June after it was shown during Xbox’s summer showcase. Insider Gaming ‘s Tom Henderson said at the time he’d heard the cost to ship the shooter was “insane” and over $400 million. Windows Central ‘s Jez Corden pushed back on that claim. He suggested the budget was lower and that accounting for the cost of The Coalition is tricky because of the work the studio does supporting teams across Xbox Game Studios.
But according to one source familiar with Xbox’s business, the cost of Gears of War: E-Day is in fact much higher. They told Kotaku it was over $500 million, and that’s before you include marketing. That would put it significantly above the reported budgets of other console-exclusive blockbusters this generation , like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 . E-Day would need to sell millions and millions of copies across all platforms to make up the difference. Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment.
Current forecasts suggest E-Day ‘s nowhere close. Alinea Analytics estimated the game sold 230,000 copies in its first week and generated just $37 million in revenue, a big chunk of which came from Game Pass subscribers paying $30 for the Premium Edition Upgrade to unlock early access. These numbers will have gone up in the two weeks since launch, but the initial momentum points to a money hole too deep for any multiplatform frag grenade to close. According to the source, E-Day was unlikely to recoup its costs no matter which platforms it came to, but as a console exclusive it could contribute to rebuilding user activity on Xbox in key areas.
Microsoft hasn’t released official metrics for E-Day ‘s performance yet, unlike it did shortly after Gears 5 released back in 2019. That entry brought in over 3 million players at launch. “The performance easily doubled the first week’s debut of Gears of War 4 and made Gears 5 the most-played Xbox Game Studios title in its first week since 2012’s Halo 4 ,” the company wrote in a press release at the time. It has so far stayed quiet on how many people have played E-Day .
Would this math have meaningfully changed if Microsoft hadn’t chosen to pull the game from PlayStation 5? It seems unlikely. Earlier this year, Alinea Analytics estimated that Gears of War: Reloaded , a remaster of the first game in the franchise and the first Gears to ever appear on PlayStation, sold 684,000 copies on PS5. Selling that many copies of E-Day on PS5 would have translated to roughly $33 million in additional revenue after subtracting Sony’s standard platform fees.
It’s possible that a well-reviewed new entry would have made an even bigger splash on PlayStation, though how much bigger is hard to tell. Reloaded was only $40 while E-Day is $70. E-Day is estimated to have sold fewer than 100,000 copies on Steam so far, though it is also available through Game Pass on PC. But no matter how you slice it, the math will not get you anywhere close to $500 million. E-Day seems poised to be a catastrophic miss for Xbox Game Studios in that regard, and an indictment of an Xbox business and game development strategy for an entire console generation.
That same math is also potentially why Xbox console exclusivity for E-Day could end up yielding greater benefits for the platform in the long run than just a few tens of millions in additional revenue. The knock-on effects are harder to measure but more significant to Xbox’s long-term health. As a big fall exclusive on Xbox, E-Day can build buzz, give some players who haven’t turned on their old Xbox Series X/S in a while a reason to come back, and potentially nudge overall engagement on the platform up in a holiday period when players are making lots of choices about what games to buy and what platforms to buy them on.
All of that could end up being worth more than a few hundred thousand additional sales on PS5. Perhaps that’s also why Forza Horizon 6 still hasn’t arrived on Sony’s console. Originally due out on PS5 sometime in 2026, the hit open-world racer’s multiplatform release has been delayed until January 2027 . Why put one of the best-selling games of the year on PS5 right as people are deciding where to buy the biggest releases of the year: Madden , EA Sports FC , NBA 2K27 , Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , and Grand Theft Auto 6 ?
That’s one argument for turning a $500 million game that will seemingly never make its money back into an Xbox Series X/S console exclusive . A recently leaked Xbox Insider survey that suggested the company is looking at leaning even further into reversing course on the recent multiplatform pivot. It was aimed specifically at users with multiple devices and trying to gain insight into how their playing habits would change under different scenarios.
“Imagine it was announced that all future title releases from every Xbox-developed gaming franchise except Call of Duty will be console-exclusive to Xbox,” the final survey question reads . “For Minecraft only, existing titles would no longer be available for purchase on PlayStation or Nintendo consoles, and would not receive any new content updates. However, there is no impact to any of the existing titles or content you already own. Nothing changes on PC in this announcement.”
It asks users what they would do in this situation: turn on the Xbox console they already own, buy a new one, switch to PC, or skip the game entirely. The feedback to questions like these could further cement Xbox’s shift back toward exclusive content. One section of the survey even hints at the possibility for franchises like The Elder Scrolls and Fallout to become console exclusives. It’s unclear where games like The Elder Scrolls 6 and Diablo 5 will end up in the future, but for now Xbox has told its players to “expect signature exclusives from us every year.”
One thing that does seem certain is that sooner or later, Xbox will need to pick a lane and stop swerving into oncoming traffic. Ex-PlayStation executive Shawn Layden called it the company’s “ Dreamcast moment .” “Either you’re going to be a platform competitive with PlayStation, which Xbox has not been competitive with PlayStation for years, but that’s not out the window,” he said last month. “You know, you can still make another run at it. And there are certain decisions you have to make around that about the platform.”
He continued, “We talked about exclusivity. We talked about, how do you incentivize third parties to support your platform in a meaningful way? This is all things around the platform business. Or you sit back and realize you are the biggest game publisher in the world.”

As oil prices crept up to their highest levels since May, President Trump accused Iran of lying about the situation in the Strait of Hormuz in order to drive up costs.
"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social . "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
The price for Brent crude, the international standard for oil, reached $112 a barrel on Thursday morning. The cost hadn't reached at least $112 since May 18.
Iran announced they had struck four vessels in the area of the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, while three others hit sea mines. All of the damaged ships were along the southern route, hugging the Omani coast, used by the U.S. to escort tankers out of the Persian Gulf, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
While the U.S. is escorting large amounts of oil out of the Gulf, it is a costly process. Overall instability in the region is also continuing to keep prices high despite increased supply since the early weeks of the war.
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group's armed forces have carried out four military operations against targets inside Saudi Arabia in the last 48 hours, including on the Defense Ministry building in Riyadh, the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and Abha International Airport.
In a video statement published on his X account, Saree claimed the attacks were carried out using ballistic missiles and drones, with direct hits on all four targets.
"The criminal Saudi enemy has carried out, during its aggression and latest escalation over the past 100 days, more than 2,900 airstrikes and missile attacks targeting civilian objects in our beloved country," he said. "Through these attacks, it has committed dozens of crimes, leaving more than 562 people killed and wounded, the majority of them women and children."
CBS News has not independently verified the claims.
The Houthis "will continue their operations deep inside Saudi Arabia in defence of our country and our people," he added.
Anti-American propaganda is a common sight on the streets of the Iranian capital, but authorities have gone a step further with their latest effort – a life-size jail cell with an actor playing President Trump languishing inside.
The 3D art installation is proving a hit with locals, who have been stopping to take selfies as well as hurl abuse at the pseudo-Trump.
Since the ongoing war began with joint American and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, Iran has ramped up its propaganda operations. In the new campaign, a mock-prison cell is suspended several stories high over Tajrish Square, in an upscale neighborhood of north Tehran.
The actor, wearing a prosthetic mask to look like Mr. Trump, paces around the cell or clutches its bars. A screen set up nearby shows messages denouncing alleged U.S. war crimes .
Tehran's municipal authorities, which are behind the campaign, have said the objective is to remind the capital's residents of Iran's demands for justice .
The Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's government in the neighboring country's spiraling civil war said Thursday that four more drones were intercepted over the capital and the hold city of Medina.
The force did not attribute the attacks to anyone, but the drones were likely launched by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who have peppered Saudi Arabia with deadly strikes in recent weeks, with many projectiles getting through the kingdom's defenses .
Earlier Thursday the Saudi coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed one drone over Riyadh, again without saying where it had come from.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting Medina or Mecca, the two holiest cities in Islam.
The shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, have run dry, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.
The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries.
"There's no more oil to discharge to China anymore," said Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude-oil analysis at the firm.
The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command.
Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty on Thursday said all options must be explored to find a political solution between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
At a press conference where he reiterated solidarity with Saudi Arabia, he stressed "the necessity of exploring all avenues for reaching political solutions."
The conflict between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis erupted in summer and has drastically escalated in recent weeks.
Egypt announced Sunday that it was prepared to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia .
A spokesman for Yemen's Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia on Thursday of targeting an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island in the Red Sea with 14 Indian nationals on board.
In a statement published on X , Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group's forces were carrying out rescue operations and would provide further information later.
"The Saudi enemy targets an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island, with 14 people of Indian nationality on board, according to preliminary information," he wrote in his post.
"This reckless act by the Saudi enemy in targeting the yacht threatens international navigation in the Red Sea, and the international community must stop the Saudi enemy from these reckless actions," said Saree.
There was no further information or other reports available to corroborate the Houthis' claim.
The Commander-in-Chief of the Iranian Army, Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, said Thursday that the country's armed forces were prepared for asymmetric warfare and satisfied with their drone capacity.
"In the previous asymmetric war, we fought the enemy with equipment that surprised them, as they received very heavy blows," he said, referring to the intense exchange of fire with the U.S. and Israel before a June ceasefire was announced. That deal, which President Trump soon declared over , failed to bring about the negotiations on Iran's nuclear program and many other issues that it provisioned, but neither side has engaged in major strikes since the summer, with fighting in the region largely shifting to the linked conflict in Yemen.
"We have reached a good level of maturity in the field of drones and unmanned systems," Hatami said. "We assure our dear people of Iran that we are in a good position."
Top European diplomats will hold talks in Istanbul Friday with their counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt during a meeting initiated by Ankara, a Turkish foreign ministry source told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Foreign ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group to discuss the Palestinian issue, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the source said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host the meeting, the first to bring together the two groups.
"The seven countries will come together for the first time in the R4+E3 format, at Turkey's initiative," the source said, indicating they would explore "opportunities for cooperation and coordination that could be put into practice ... in the coming period."
In chairing the meeting, Fidan was expected to focus on the international community "increasing pressure on Israel" in response to its settlement expansion and its "encouragement of settler terrorism," the source AFP.

articles.title_orig: Attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd airport kills two people
articles.title_zh: Attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd airport kills two people
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says that the number of people killed in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam has risen to two – a Saudi national and an Indian resident.
The GACA said in a statement on Thursday that eight people were wounded in Wednesday’s attack and that operations at the airport had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal.
Separately on Wednesday, two people were killed after Saudi air defences intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield, the Ministry of Energy said.
The attack are the latest in a series of assaults on Saudi infrastructure as conflict intensifies between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Last week, the kingdom reported that a projectile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 11 killed one person and injured 11. On October 10, the civil aviation authority reported that a separate attack on the same airport killed 12 people and injured more than 300.
The Houthis on Thursday claimed to have carried out numerous attacks on Saudi infrastructure over the last 48 hours, including targeting King Fahd International Airport. Other targets included Abha International Airport, the Saudi defence ministry in Riyadh and facilities belonging to Saudi ‌Aramco in Yanbu, according to the Houthis.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed group, meanwhile, said four drones had been intercepted and destroyed in the regions of Riyadh and Medina.
Reuters and AFP cited sources as saying Saudi Aramco had ordered staff to evacuate from its headquarters in Dhahran, which was hit by a Houthi attack earlier in the month .
The reported evacuation came a day after the US State Department ordered diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia. There were also plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
The US embassy in Riyadh had issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Tesla stock slips despite Q3 earnings beat, better-than-expected capex spend
articles.title_zh: Tesla stock slips despite Q3 earnings beat, better-than-expected capex spend
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Tesla ( TSLA ) reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings, with its free cash flow and capex spending coming in ahead of Wall Street estimates.
Tesla reported Q3 revenue of $28.05 billion vs. Bloomberg consensus of $28.13 billion. Tesla posted adjusted EPS of $0.48 vs. the $0.44 estimate, with adjusted EBITDA of $3.90 billion vs. $3.66 billion.
Tesla stock pared some of its earlier losses, with Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein claiming the market was reacting to "capacity constraints in the company's auto and battery growth, which could slow near-term growth."
But that might not be the whole story. Tesla reported free cash flow of $1.53 billion vs. an estimated -$4.92 billion, with capital expenditures climbing to $4.732 billion vs. an estimated $7.96 billion for the quarter.
On the earnings call, Tesla updated its full-year capex guidance to $20 billion from $25 billion previously. Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the savings would come from "managing our capital deployment efficiently, and plan to fund [capex] primarily from our cash flows from operations," he said.
"I think capex is actually ending up being a little lower than we anticipated, but we'll start to become more meaningful next year. And then noticeable in the tens of billions in '28," CEO Elon Musk said on the call.
Roundhill CEO Dave Mazza posits the cutting capex means the Tesla isn't transitioning fast enough to an AI-focused company betting on robotaxis, Optimus robots, and compute.
Tesla revealed its Optimus robot started production at its Fremont factory. "While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product," the company said in its earnings release.
"I would expect that it takes us probably at least a year — maybe a little longer — to get to that annualized rate [1 million units], to get to 20,000 units a week," Musk said on the earnings call. Musk added that Tesla may release an Optimus demo video in about a month, stressing that he didn't want the robot's movements to be preplanned.
Regarding its other AI efforts, Tesla said it plans to reach 400 MW of AI training compute by the end of the year. Tesla said its active FSD (full self-driving) subscriptions climbed to 1.74 million.
"The biggest driver of demand is full self-driving," Musk said regarding vehicle sales.
"The Cybercab fleet in Austin has grown by a factor of 10," Musk added while discussing Tesla's robotaxi fleet. He added, "I don't think there's any company in the world that can match our scale with autonomous vehicles."
Musk also stirred the pot recently with comments about a possible tie-up with SpaceX, his other company.
"I think both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call Tuesday night. "At the request of shareholders, and these special committees consist of independent directors. And because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees."
He added , "I don't think we should necessarily assume that I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty. And I think that would be overstating it. Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes."
On the Tesla call, Musk briefly touched on it but added nothing new. "With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday [Tuesday]," Musk said.
Tesla reported Q3 deliveries of 486,532, down 2% from a year ago but well ahead of the Bloomberg consensus of 463,000. Energy storage deployments came in at 13.7 GWh, up from 12.5 GWh a year ago and Q2's 13.5 GWh.
Tesla began commercial Cybercab service in Austin on Sept. 3, but federal regulators have questions. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) issued Tesla a special order with 21 requests on how it self-certified the Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or pedals, as compliant with federal safety standards. Tesla asked for an extension to Nov. 20. NHTSA granted 30 days instead , making answers due Oct. 30.
Tesla also finally revealed its long-delayed Roadster last Thursday at SpaceX's ( SPCX ) facility in Waco, Texas. The car used cold-gas thrusters to jump over several Teslas, including a Semi. Tesla said the Roadster hit 0-60 mph in 0.81 seconds in a test at the event, and Musk said production starts in 2028.
Deepwater's Gene Munster called it an "engineering flex" with little commercial value, and Morningstar expects the Roadster to sell fewer than 2,000 units a year.

articles.title_orig: US weekly jobless claims near 57-year lows, underscore labor market stability
articles.title_zh: US weekly jobless claims near 57-year lows, underscore labor market stability
articles.content_orig:
Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates . Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

articles.title_orig: Meta's credit risk indicator jumps to record high after results
articles.title_zh: Meta's credit risk indicator jumps to record high after results
articles.content_orig:
Meta has signed up to about $825bn in future leases and contracts, most of them for the data centres and computing power behind its AI push. The figures are in its quarterly filing with US regulators, dated October 22, 2026.
Bloomberg reported the total by adding together three items in the filing. In July, the news agency put Meta’s commitments at almost $700bn.
The largest item is $454.5bn in contracts that Meta cannot cancel. According to the filing, these mostly cover cloud capacity bought from other companies, plus servers and network equipment. They also include energy supply for data centres and hardware for Reality Labs, its virtual reality unit.
About $45.9bn of those contracts fall due in the rest of 2026, and $121.4bn in 2027.
Meta also has $355.7bn in leases that have not started yet, so they do not appear on its balance sheet. They cover data centres, energy infrastructure, shared server space and network equipment. The leases begin between now and 2036 and run for up to 30 years.
The third item is a deal to buy up to $14.7bn of cloud capacity over five years. That amount could shrink if the cloud provider sells the capacity to other customers, the filing says.
The commitments come on top of heavy spending now. In its third-quarter results on Wednesday, Meta said capital expenditure, including finance lease payments, reached $34.9bn in the three months to September 30. Free cash flow was negative $2.1bn.
Meta now expects to spend $135bn to $145bn this year, narrowing an earlier range of $130bn to $145bn.
“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” said Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, in the results statement.
At the same time, Meta plans to create non-voting Class C shares , effective from January 19, 2027. The filing says the company expects to use them to sell new shares to investors in the future.
Meta’s shares fell about 3% in pre-market trading on Thursday. The cost of insuring Meta’s debt against default also hit a record. Its five-year credit default swaps reached about 119 basis points, according to ICE Data Services figures cited in market reports.

Semiconductor stocks fell in premarket trading on Thursday as a major equipment supplier cited supply chain constraints on its earnings call.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( SOXX ) tumbled 4% amid investor concerns that such limitations could potentially hurt chip sales. AI chip heavyweight Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Qualcomm ( QCOM ) dropped more 2%, while Marvell ( MRVL ) and Intel ( INTC ) shares were down 4% and 5%, respectively.
Chip developer Broadcom ( AVGO ) shares also fell more than 3%. Despite reaching an all-time high earlier this year, the stock is now flat year to date.
Meanwhile, memory and storage highfliers Micron Technology ( MU ) and Sandisk ( SNDK ) were also in red territory.
Shares of the wafer equipment maker Lam Research ( LRCX ) fell as much as 10% after CFO Doug Bettinger said the quarterly revenue guidance of $8.6 billion "would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints," which the company is actively managing.
Other equipment makers Applied Materials ( AMAT ) fell 6%, while ASML ( ASML ) declined 3%.
Semiconductor stocks have been volatile in recent sessions as concerns over AI funding have weighed on the sector. Semiconductor companies have been a key beneficiary of the artificial intelligence build-out.
On Thursday, the overall stock market was set to open lower as oil prices surged, raising expectations that the Federal Reserve may have to keep tightening monetary policy this year.
